common_name: Macrantha Yesterday Today Tomorrow (Giant-Flowered Royal Purple Brunfelsia)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once nights stay reliably above 50°F, in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; 'Macrantha' can be trained as a large shrub or, with staking and selective pruning of lower shoots, a small single-trunk patio tree.

directions: Set new plants out in spring in humus-rich, acidic, evenly moist but well-drained soil, sited where afternoon sun is filtered. 'Macrantha' is grown chiefly for flower size rather than fragrance — each bloom expands to nearly three inches across, noticeably larger than the standard species or 'Floribunda', and still runs through the classic deep-purple-to-lavender-to-near-white progression that gives yesterday-today-tomorrow its name, so all three color stages show at once on a mature plant. Growth is more open and upright than the dwarf selections, reaching roughly five feet in as many years, and responds well to a post-bloom shaping prune that keeps flowering wood renewed near the plant's interior. Because bloom is heaviest on partial-shade sites with consistent moisture, mulch well and avoid letting the root zone dry between waterings; all plant parts are toxic if eaten, so keep it away from pets prone to chewing dropped berries.

common_name: Athens Blue Princess Flower (Compact University of Georgia Selection)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed, in slightly acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter; this selection stays noticeably more compact than seed-grown princess flower, making it a better fit for smaller borders and large containers.

directions: Plant in organically rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil with morning sun and light afternoon shade in the hottest climates. 'Athens Blue' was selected at the University of Georgia trial gardens for a tighter, more floriferous habit than typical seed-grown Tibouchina urvilleana, carrying the same intensely saturated violet-blue flowers over a longer bloom window from spring into fall rather than concentrating color mainly in late summer. Its smaller mature footprint suits foundation plantings and large patio pots more readily than the straight species, though winter protection or container culture is still needed outside the warmest parts of zone 9. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and deadhead spent flowers to keep the compact form dense and well covered in bloom.
sources: University of Georgia Center for Applied Nursery Research
North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after last frost in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun with some afternoon relief in hot climates; give it more sun than other tibouchinas to keep the silvery leaf color from turning plain green.

directions: Plant in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun, holding back afternoon shade to only the harshest summer sites. Silver-leaf princess flower is grown as much for its broad, velvety, silver-green foliage with pale undersides as for its flowers — the leaves alone set it apart from the glossier-leaved Tibouchina urvilleana at a glance, and older leaves turn warm orange before dropping, adding a second season of color. Rich violet-purple flowers cluster on upright terminal spikes from summer into fall, later in the season than most garden tibouchinas, on a shrub that becomes noticeably more tree-like with age than its smaller relatives. Feed lightly through the growing season and shelter from hard freezes, since like other tender tibouchinas it dies back hard below the mid-20s and is best grown in large containers outside the warmest microclimates of zone 9.
